title: Beyblade HK Leaderboard: Rankings, Events & Community in Hong Kong

spans.text: Beyblade HK leaderboard is the search Hong Kong players run when they want one answer: where do I stand? The honest answer is that the city has more than one board, and each measures something different. Takara Tomy Asia runs the official G1, G2 and G3 tournament circuit, community platforms turn tournament results into Elo ratings, and the BeyHK app keeps a live ladder built from confirmed matches between local players. The number that means "won a regional title" on one board means "played five confirmed matches this season" on another.

This guide compares the three boards side by side, explains the rating maths behind them, shows what actually moves your position, and tells you how to check your standing today. Everything below reflects the current season and the way each board works right now.
Key takeaways
Hong Kong has three kinds of Beyblade X leaderboards: the official G1, G2 and G3 circuit, community Elo boards, and in-app match ladders. Each one counts different results.
Official battles use a four-point system: an Xtreme Finish earns 3 points, Knockout and Burst Finishes earn 2 each, a Survivor Finish earns 1, and the first player to 4 points wins the battle.
In-app ladders rate you with Glicko-2, a system that rewards wins over stronger opponents and grows less certain about your skill when you stop playing.
Getting listed is fast: enter one tracked tournament, or log five confirmed matches and the app ladder places you in a tier.
What is a Beyblade HK leaderboard?

A Beyblade HK leaderboard is any ranked list that orders Hong Kong Beyblade X players by results. The official circuit runs G1, G2 and G3 tournaments in Hong Kong, community sites such as TopDeck publish Elo ratings from tracked tournaments, and the BeyHK app maintains a live Glicko-2 ladder from confirmed matches.

That one sentence hides a real choice. Tournament boards reward peak performance on the day, so a player who travels well can sit high with a modest match count. A match ladder rewards volume and consistency, because every confirmed game moves your number. Neither is wrong. They answer different questions, and most competitive players in the city end up on more than one board.

The boards also differ in who can enter them. The official circuit requires registration for listed events. Community Elo boards count only games played in tracked tournaments. An in-app ladder counts the matches you already play at your usual venue, which is why it is the natural first board for a new player.
The three leaderboards Hong Kong players actually use
Hong Kong players currently track their standing on three kinds of boards, and each counts different results.
The official circuit: G1, G2 and G3
The official Hong Kong circuit is Takara Tomy Asia's G1, G2 and G3 tournament series, and your standing there comes from how far you go in each event. The
event page

lists Hong Kong tournaments alongside the current regulation document, the 11th edition dated October 2025, which defines the legal parts and battle procedures for the season. Formats and dates change by season, so treat the event page as the single source of truth for what is coming next and for the results of the last event.
Community Elo boards
Community boards convert tournament results into an Elo number, the same rating maths that chess federations made famous.
TopDeck's Elo leaderboard

for Beyblade X ranks players who compete in tracked tournaments, and you appear there once you have rated games on record. Long-running community organisations such as the World Beyblade Organization also maintain league boards, though entry rules and coverage differ by region, so check a board's own listing criteria before expecting your local event to count.
In-app ladders

In-app ladders build a ranking from everyday confirmed matches instead of tournament days. Both players confirm the result, and the rating moves after every confirmed game. The system behind most modern ladders is the
Glicko rating system

, developed by statistician Mark Glickman in 1995, which pairs every player's rating with a deviation value that shows how certain the system is about it. New players move quickly in both directions. Long inactive stretches widen the deviation, which is the system saying it is less sure about your number, and that lets sharper swings happen once you return to the table.

Two practical consequences follow. First, an Xtreme Finish is worth as much as a burst plus a spin finish combined, which is why attack combos that can land it shape so many metagame debates. Second, because a battle ends at 4 points, one mistake rarely decides a match. You need to convert finishes repeatedly across battles, and that consistency is exactly what tournament standings reward.

If you want a number that impresses at a tournament, the official circuit carries the most weight. If you want a number that reflects your weekly form, an in-app ladder updates faster and counts far more of the games you already play. Most players keep a foot in both worlds.
How to climb a Beyblade HK leaderboard
Climbing any Beyblade HK leaderboard comes down to three habits, and none of them require spending money beyond your gear.
Play matches that count

Casual launches with friends move nothing on any board. The app ladder counts only confirmed matches, where both players accept the result, and the current threshold is five confirmed matches before you appear in the standings. Community boards count only tracked tournament games. If your goal is a number that means something, spend your table time on results that register.
Beat players rated above you

Every rating system rewards upsets more than expected wins. Under Glicko-2, beating a player whose rating sits well above yours moves your number much further than beating someone far below you, where a win adds little and a loss costs a lot. Target opponents slightly above your band instead of farming easy games. The app ladder also bands players into tiers, currently Bronze below 1400, Silver from 1400 to 1599, Gold from 1600 to 1799, and Platinum at 1800 and above, which makes it easy to find the right sparring partners at your level.
Mind the season mechanics

Ladders reset. When a season closes, ratings recalibrate for the new season, while your match history and a season recap stay on your profile. Seasons can also carry requirements. If the season asks for an in-person meet-up check or a pre-match line-up and the pair does not complete it, the match logs as unranked and your rating does not move. Read the season notice before your first match rather than after your first surprise.
How to check your standing today

Checking each board takes minutes once you know where to look. For the official circuit, open Takara Tomy Asia's event page and look at the Hong Kong listings for dates, venues and the latest results. For community Elo, the TopDeck board linked above updates as tracked tournaments report. For the app ladder, open the Rank tab: the
ranking page
explains what the tab shows, the
events page
lists upcoming tournament play across the city, and
how the app works
walks through logging and confirming a match end to end.
If one of your matches shows as unranked, check the season requirements first. The most common cause is a missing meet-up check, not a bug in the ranking.
Conclusion
Conclusion:

A Beyblade HK leaderboard is only as meaningful as the results behind it, so pick the board that matches how you actually play. Chasing titles means the official G1 to G3 circuit. Tournament regulars should build an Elo history on community boards. If you play weekly at a venue, the BeyHK app ladder turns those matches into a Hong Kong ranking after five confirmations. The concrete next step takes one evening: register for the next listed event, or log and confirm your next five matches and watch your name land on the ladder.
FAQ

summary.text: How do I get on a Beyblade HK leaderboard?

spans.text: Three routes: register for a listed G1, G2 or G3 event on the official circuit; play in community tournaments that feed a tracked Elo board; or log confirmed matches on the app ladder, which lists you after five confirmations.

summary.text: How many matches do I need before I appear on the ladder?

spans.text: Five confirmed matches is the current threshold on the app ladder. Community Elo boards need rated tournament games, and each board's own listing page states exactly how many it requires.

summary.text: Do Hong Kong Beyblade X ratings reset?

spans.text: App ladders run in seasons. When a season closes, ratings recalibrate for the new season while your match history and season recap stay on your profile, so a reset is a fresh start rather than a wipe.

summary.text: How much does it cost to compete on a Beyblade HK leaderboard?

spans.text: It depends on the organizer. Logging confirmed matches on the app ladder costs nothing beyond your gear. Community events are often free or charge a small venue fee, and official events may charge an entry fee that varies by event. Check each event's listing before you register, because fees and prize structures change by season.

summary.text: Can beginners and younger players join ranked play?

spans.text: Yes. Several Hong Kong event formats are designed for newer players, and past seasons have included junior categories, with each event listing stating its age groups. On the app ladder every player starts near the middle of the range, and the deviation system means your early results place you quickly.
